The powers of the civil service examiners as a board under sections 7 and 15, both inclusive, of the Civil Service Act, shall be vested in and exercised by the commission, and for the purposes of the said sections, either one of the members of the commission may exercise any function or power vested by said sections or any of them, in the chairman of the board.
The present board has a chairman, and there are certain things which the chairman is authorized to do that the other members of the board are not authorized to do, and we wish to give either of the new commissioners the powers that the chairman has. Then clause 3 of section 12 would read :
The provisions of the said sections shall, so far as they are applicable, apply to examinations under this Act mutatis mutandis.
These sections chiefly regard irregularities in examinations and improper actions. We wish the new commission to have the powers of the old board. Then I would take the present clause 2 of section 12 and make it clause 4 of the new section 12, and I would amend it in the way we were speaking of a few minutes ago.
Such further examiners as are deemed necessary may be appointed by the commission.
I do not think we need say anything further. I will have these put in proper form in the reprinted Bill for the third reading.

I quite agree with the minster in all those amendments. When we see them in print we may think of some other improvements. No doubt you will have to abolish the old board. We have good authority for saying that you cannot put new wine into old bottles. You have now a board of Civil Service Commissioners who have certain duties, and when you form your new commission you cannot have two boards, you cannot amalgamate them. It is necessary that the old board shall disappear.

I have been discussing and preparing amendments which will affect sections 3, 4, 24 and 38. These sections depend on one another, and amendments in any one of them will affect more or less the others. I ask that they stand until I can get these amendments worked out. I would like to say that I will prepare one general clause in regard to the employees of the House of Commons, the Senate and the library, in which the Governor in Council will riot deal with them in the same way that he deals with the other departmental officers. The amendments which I propose to make to sections 3 and 4 in regard to the employees of the House, will, I hope, cover the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. James Division, Montreal (Mr. Ger-vais).

I hope the minister will take into consideration the amend-



ment that was suggested to-night about not approaching the commissioners.

I have to thank hon. members for the way in 'which they have expedited the progress of the Bill, and I will now ask that the committee rise and report progress.
Progress reported.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext: I understood that my hon. friend from Prince, P.E.I., desired to say something with reference to public works in his province.

I wanted to ask particularly about the repairs at Tignish. I have brought the case of Tignish to the attention of the House several times during the session. Petitions were sent from responsible men in Tignish, from Caraquet in New Brunsiwick and from the West Prince Board of Trade asking that Tignish harbour be enlarged to allow the fishing fleets to find a place of refuge. The minister said the department were taking the matter into consideration. He said that they had received a petition from the Alberton and West Prince Board of Trade and also from the people of Gloucester county, and the matter was in the hands of the resident engineer for a report which they would have to await before any opinion could be expressed on the matter.

There is an item in the Main Estimates which has been passed for certain work at Tignish consisting of general repairs to breakwaters, in the way of planking, fenders, piling, floor stringers, ballasting and brush work. With regard to the further improvements which have been asked for no conclusion has been arrived at. There has been expended in various years at Tignish quite a large amount of money. I understand that further improvements are urged by people who are interested in the harbour, and the most I can say to my hon. friend at present is that the matter is still under consideration.

This is a matter of very great importance to the fishermen there and there is no port along the coast of New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island where the fishing fleet can seek refuge. The question should be decided without any delay. Having brought this matter to the attention of the minister in February last I had hoped that by this time some decision would have been arrived at. This is not a matter that can be deferred indefinitely. It should receive the atten-Mr. SAM. HUGHES.
tion of the department at once and I have no doubt that it would meet the approval of the minister if he would look into the situation. I trust that before the House closes the minister will have an amount in the supplementary estimates to provide for this work being done. Along the whole coast there are a number of public works needed. When the minister talks of so much money being expended at Tignish I would say to him that since confederation the whole sum expended on public works in Prince Edward Island is very little more than three times the amount expended in Nova Scotia in one year. We have a big coast line around Prince Edward Island and there are a great many public works needed. In my own county there have been very small amounts appropriated for urgent public works. Our fisheries cannot be carried on without breakwaters and wharfs to enable the fleets to bring in their product and to shelter the boats. I would like to impress on the minister the necessity of having a' vote for the improvement of Tignish harbour and of having the work started and completed before the bad weather comes on when it is most necessary that these boats should have shelter. I would like also to call the minister's attention to the necessity of a wharf at Higgin's shore.
The necessities at Higgin's shore have not been brought to my attention.
They were brought to the minister's attention on December 16.
If they have been it has escaped my memory.

On December 16, I asked the minister if he had received a request for an extension of the wharf at Higgin's shore to make it available for small trading vessels and the minister replied :
Yes, a request has been made and the matter is under consideration.
The minister is not paying much attention to the needs of Prince Edward Island in the matter of public works. Since confederation only one and a half million dollars have been spent in the whole province of Prince Edward Island for public works, and on the whole coast line of Prince county, for several years past there has only been an average expenditure of $11,000 per year.
How much was spent in Conservative days ?

About $11,000 per year in Prince county and it is about the same under the Liberal administration. At Higgins shore the people are ten or fifteen miles away from the railway and certain inexpensive improvements are absolutely needed there to give accommodation. Then as to Hubbard's cove, was not a petition
11681	JUNE 30, 1908	11682
received from the people there accompanied by a chart showing the coast line and explaining the necessity of a wharf at that point?

I hope my bon. friend will not think I am discourteous to him, but there being no items in the estimates now before the committee for these works I have not with me to-night the information which he seeks.
I can understand that, but at the same time I have brought every one of these matters to the attention of the minister at different times during this session.
And no doubt I gave the hon. gentleman answers.

Yes, but your answer was last December that the case of Tignish harbour and Higgin's shore were under consideration and your answer is the same to-night. These works are badly needed for the convenience of the fishermen, and as seven months have elapsed since the minister first told me he was considering it, it is time the people should know when they will get relief.

There is no one more desirous than I am of affording to the people living along the coasts of the martitime provinces, along the shores oif the great lakes and of our navigable waters generally, every facility for the carrying on of their means of livelihood in the way of improvement to harbours and protection for fishermen. My hon. friend will recognize that there are innumerable demands from all sections of the country, and were I to comply with all these demands the estimates would have risen to such proportion as to cause parliament to think that I was not justified in asking for such a large expenditure. I have brought the best judgment I could to bear on the information at my disposal in order to provide for these works which are at present most necessary. As to the works to which my hon. friend has called attention and which are not now provided for, careful inquiry will be made and action taken on the basis of the reports furnished me. I do not admit for a moment that Prince Edward Island is receiving unjust treatment from this parliament or this government. In the matter of building branches and extensions of the Intercolonial railway
We are not considering the Intercolonial Railway now; we are talking about your department.

But my hon. friend must consider and the people of Prince Edward Island must consider and the people of the country will consider the expenditures made on the various public services in the one province or the other. I
believe there is a disposition on the part of parliament, as there is on the part of the government, to treat Prince Edward Island not only fairly, but, as a smaller province, even generously.
I do not see it.
The hon. gentleman said that in Conservative days the average expenditure upon the harbours of Prince Edward Island was about $11,000 per year.
What I said was that the expenditure in the county of Prince was $11,000 per year.

Well, I do not know what the expenditure in Prince Edward Island was in Conservative days, but in the main estimates that are before parliament I have $85,000 for wharfs and improvements in that province, and I am inclined to think that when the supplementary estimates are brought down my hon. friend will see a still further disposition on the part of the government to deal justly with Prince Edward Island as well as with other provinces of the Dominion. With regard to the particular works to which the hon. gentleman has called my attention, all I can say is that they are under consideration. When I say they are under consideration, I mean that they will be carefully considered with the view of meeting, in this and all other respects, the reasonable requirements of the people of Prince Edward Island.

The minister has said that I complained about certain things when I merely pointed out to him that certain works require to be constructed in Prince Edward Island. This I did many months ago and he then gave exactly the same reply. He tells us that he is dealing with the island with a lavish hand and that he has $85,000 in the estimates for public works in that province. But the bulk of that item is made up of a $50,000 vote for a breakwater in Summerside harbour. If the hon. gentleman were familiar with the history of that breakwater, he would not boast of that expenditure. Away back in 1900, when I was running an election in Prince county, the Liberals got out a big poster, a few days before the polling, telling the people what an immense sum they were going to spend on this breakwater and what an amount of employment it would give a great number of men. Well, we have had that vote in the estimates every session since 1900. The work was to have been completed about a year and a half or two years after the vote was first put in, so that I do not think the minister can take very much credit out of this $85,000 when he subtracts $50,000 from it. However that work is going on, and I presume will be completed in a few years. But what I do complain of is the small amount of money we have been annually get*-

ting to meet the necessities now apparent of onr very large coast line and which need instant remedy. The minister says he is not prepared to give the information asked. All I can say is that it is customary to give such information, especially when the matter has been brought to the attention of the minister before and when the necessities have been urged on the minister by the different boards of trade. If the minister inquires he will find that he had ample data in his department to have enabled him to give the information to-night and to have justified him in promising the people on this coast additional harbour accommodation at Tignish. One of his engineers went down there and said the work could readily be done for about $20,000. If the hon. mnister is so willing to do everything possible for Prince Edward Island, he ought not to hesitate giving a first-class harbour to the people along that coast, which would only cost $20,000. In reply to an inquiry I made on February 11, the minister informed me that:
The proposed improvements leave no doubt that the space between the breakwaters would scour out so as to carry a depth of from four to five feet at low water which will be sufficient for the class of boats usually making use of the harbour. The estimated cost of the work would be $20,000.
That is about as much information as to the work itself and its cost as I can give to-night.

But you did not have information and were not prepared to say what would be done. When the minister had this information on February 11, I think he should have been able to-night to say whether this work would go on or not. There are a number of other places to which I would call his attention. He can look them up in his department and possibly will give me the favour of an interview when we can talk these matters over more intimately. I would call his attention to some other places which have been pointed out to him by the people of Prince county and also by myself in this House. There is other work needed at Mimminegash and also at Kildare, concerning which a petition was sent the minister. There is a long coast line there which is absolutely bare and it is frequented by some forty or fifty boats. The work is not of very great magnitude and would be of great service to the fishermen. Petitions have also been sent in for the dredging and improving of Bray harbour. There is also needed at West Point further accommodation for the fishermen there, and a light is much needed on the breakwater at that point. What is being done with the ferry wharf at Table Point, Lennox island ? I believe that work is still going on.
I am informed that there is no work going on there at present.
What has been done ?

I haye no memo, to-night with regard to that. The requirements of the island have been carefully considered and the additional provision which will now be made for various works will be made in the supplementary, estimates. My hon friend could not expect me to anticipate what may be the action of the government with regard to the different public works until the estimates have been passed by council and submitted to parliament.

The minister is wrongly informed. On May 14, in answer to a question of mine, he said that the contract had been let for building the Lennox island ferry wharf, that the contract price for the landing wharf is $625 and that $150 had been paid on account. There must be some further expenditure as the work is not completed.

I would be very happy to give the information, but if my hon. friend desires information regarding any particular work, he should have given me a memo. I have already answered when he put the question in the House. I do not come here tonight prepared to answer any questions except those which pertain to the items under consideration. We have certain items in the main estimates, and it will be my pleasure to answer fully regarding them, but I cannot be expected to have the information offhand as to any other work not included in the estimates.
If the minister cannot give me the information to-night I shall have to have a personal interview with him.
I notice that this Bue-touche contract is by day labour and a man named Cormier has been foreman. Who is responsible in such a case for the purchase of supplies?
For supplies such as lumber, iron work, &c., the foreman of course must act under the direction of the resident engineer whom we hold responsible.
Are tenders asked?
In this particular case the larger part of the work is dredging.
There is $55 for stone supplied by Mr. Irving, a lawyer.
He is engaged in other business besides law.
Would tenders be asked for the stone or would the foreman take the responsibility?

There were no tenders, it would be purchased by the resident engineer who is responsible for the price. The expenditure to October last was $2,917, and it is expected to be completed this year by this vote, making the total cost about $5,000.

Campbellton wharf-extension and repairs,
Is this for the completion of Mr. Glover's contract and will it complete the work?
This is Mr. Glover's contract. We will require a further appropriation in the Supplementaries. The work is to be completed by December, 1909, and the contract price for the extension is $35,475.
Was not a wharf built there two or three years ago at a cost of $35,000? I understand this money is to extend that wharf.

Yes, an extension of the new deep water wharf at the eastern end. The extension is 314 feet long and 45 feet wide and there is dredging required as well. Eight tenders were received of which the highest was $44,469. The chief engineer's estimate was $38,000, and the contract was awarded to the lowest tenderer.
The report of the department speaks of a contract with Glover for the building of a wharf 200 feet long and 45 feet wide as a western extension at $16,000. Is that completed?

That is the old contract and it is completed.
Caraquet wharf, approach, ice-breakers, &c., $3,90(1.
How much have the wharf and approaches cost to date?

The total expenditure in connection with this up to March 31, 1907, was $68,345. The present work is for the completion of the third ice-breaking pier for the efficient protection of the outer end of the wharf and the total expenditure for this work is supposed to be $5,400.
Mr, CROCKET. This is the wharf for which an appropriation was first voted in 1902, and concerning which not long ago the member for Gloucester ((Mr. Turgeon) stated in this House that the time had not yet come to demonstrate the utility of that wharf. I have already stated that the wharf had not been used for any purpose since its completion on March 31, 1905, except drying fish nets. I believe that this year one small boat did land at the wharf, it seems to me that the people of other constituencies and sections of the country where there is much need of public works have reason to complain of the expenditure of such a large sum as this for a wharf which, as the member for the constituency in 1908 admits, has not found any use up to this time.
Has the government acquired title to the railway leading from the highway down to the wharf ?
Yes, the title has been acquired.
From whom ?
I do not know.

From the different parties interested. All the titles have been got, some from Blackballs, and some from other parties. The road crosses four or five farms and the different parties have given titles to their property. These are in the Department of Justice, I suppose.
Who paid for the construction of the road ?
The department. It was made under the supervision of the resident engineer.
The department built a quarter of a mile of road down a side hill to reach the wharf, and charged the expense to the wharf ?
Roadway to the wharf is always provided.
I have information from Gloucester county that there is a claim against the government for compensation for a portion of this roadway.
What is the amount ?

I am informed that the claimant is Mrs. Blanche Blackhall, widow of Richard Blackhall. It appears that the land through which this roadway passes was formerly owned by a man named Wilson, who abandoned possession of the property and removed to Scotland about half a century ago. Blackhall subsequently went into possession of the property-
Apart from the details of the title, what is the amount of the claim ?
It is $400. I will state to the minister the information I have-
It really is not necessary ; the matter goes through the Department of Justice.

I will state it whether the minister deems it necessary or not. Blackhall went into possession of the property, occupied it for twenty years and established a statutory title by possession. When this wharf was completed, negotiations were had with Blackhall-or, it may be, with his widow after his death-to acquire title to the property. I am informed that the engineer recommended that the property was worth $400, and that the department agreed upon Mrs. Blackhall executing a deed and affidavit setting forth the occupation for twenty years, to pay over the same. The deed and affidavit were executed. But, subsequently, and not very

long ago, the member for the county Informed Mrs. Blackhall that the Justice Department had advised against the paying of the compensation agreed upon, for the reason that one Wilson who was the son of a cousin of the former owner of this property, had bobbed up as a claimant to the land, notwithstanding that he had taken no proceedings for over a score of years to dispossess the Blackballs. And the member for the county (Mr. Turgeon) informed Mrs. Blackhall that if she would pay, or agree to pay, Wilson $100, the matter might be put through and the amount paid. Now, this Wilson, I understand, is a collector of customs, one of the appointees of the hon. member for Gloucester, and it is reported to me that he is a very active political partisan of my hon. friend. And it does seem to me that, if these negotiations were carried on with Blackhall or Mrs. Blackhall, as alleged, and if there was an agreement to pay her $400 on the execution of the deed and affidavit, it is not very creditable to find the member for the county, backed up by the Justice Department, at this time endeavouring to land $100 for a political friend who does not seem to have any legal claim to the property in the way described. I do hope the minister will have the matte? investigated and see that the rights of Mrs. Blackhall are protected, and that the agreement which seems to have been entered into will be carried out.	.

I am sorry that my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket) is not well informed on the facts of this case. So far as friendship is concerned, Mr. Blackhall was all his life, a most particular friend of mine, and his widow and family had all my sympathies. When the road in question was to be taken over by the department, nobody in the county, probably, ever thought of any claim being filed against the widow. The department had dealings in the matter and agreed to pay $400 or thereabouts. While the payment was delayed, the family of Wilson brought in a claim of which I never heard before. One Mr. Wilson filed his claim in the Department of Justice and so delayed proceedings.
I remember one day, on her invitation I called on Mrs. Blackhall and she admitting to me that there might be a certain claim on the part of the Wilsons on a portion of the land taken over by the resident engineer for $400. She was anxious for an immediate settlement. I did advise her that, if she thought her claim was not perfect, it would be better to give up $100 of the full claim and settle the matter at once and avoid further delay in legal proceedings. That, of course, was a matter for her to consider. The case has been before the Department of Justice, hut is not yet decided. They have an agent in the county and correspondence I Mr. CROCKET.
has been exchanged between him and the department. So far as political feiendship is concerned I owe both families all consideration.
The member admits, I understand, that the department did agree to pay Mrs Blackhall $400 upon the execution of a deed of her title-
No, she agreed with me to let the other claimant have $100-
Did not the hon. gentleman state-
I am reported to have stated, but I am giving now what I said.

What the hon. member (Mr. Turgeon) stated was perfectly clear. The department agreed to pay $400 for property of which it was represented Mrs. Blackhall was the owner. At that time the claim of Wilson was not heard of. But subsequently, that claim was presented to the department by Wilson. Naturally the deputy Minister of Justice would look into the matter and consider how he could get a good title or whether it would be necessary to expropriate. Then it was, as the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) said, Mrs. Blackhall admitted that perhaps Wilson did have a good claim, and she agreed to allow $100 to secure a settlement of her claim. I do not think there is anything to warrant hon. gentlemen in suggesting that the hon. member for Gloucester has acted in any but a proper manner in this case. Surely, as soon as it came to the notice of the Justice Department that there was another claim, it was the business of the deputy minister to stay his hand and not pay out public money until he was sure there was a perfect title.
Was not the agreement made by the minister with Mrs. Blackhall to pay her $400 upon the completion of her title?
Assuming she could give a title.

The whole matter was referred to the agent of the Justice Department at Bathurst, Mr. Byrne, who had full knowledge af the facts, and this agreement was made with full knowledge of the fact that he was getting just as good a title as Mr. Blackhall had, a title established by occupation for over twenty years. She was to receive $400, and then this man Wilson, who never had made any claim to the property and could not establish anv title
Does the hon. gentleman know that he could not establish a title?

He could not establish a title against the occupation that Mrs. Blackball proved to the satisfaction of the agent of the Justice Department ; open and adverse occupation for over twenty years gave a title which the department agreed to accept. It seems strange that this man, who was a son of a cousin of the former-owner, should be recognized by the Justice Department, and that the member for the county should make a demand upon Mrs. Blackball to pay his friend Wilson $100 and the matter would go through.	.

I did not make a demand upon Mrs. Blackball. She avowed to me herself that possibly the Wilson family had a title, that the twenty years was merely a matter of memory. There was no deed showing possession at all, it was merely a matter of memory-it might be nineteen years or twenty-one years.
Does the minister propose to expend $08,000 on a wharf that has never been used and never likely to be used?

As I understand it, when this wharf was constructed an application was made by the people of the locality for certain dredging work to be done, and owing to the demand of other places, the dredging work has not yet been done. But I am glad to be able to inform the committee, or those members of it who take an interest in the proper and reasonable development of that section of Gloucester county, that the dredging will be done, and before long ocean steamers can come to this wharf and do the business for which it is intended this wharf shall make provision. There is another thing which is needed, and which my hon. friend who represents Gloucester so efficiently is urging, and that is that some provision should be made for the building of a spur line from the Caraquet Railway down to this wharf There will then be a very efficient and valuable deep water wharf giving connection between the railway and the steamers, and I am sure that when the dredging is done, even if the spur is not built-though we expect it will be-it will be found that this wharf will afford very much needed accommodation.
Mr. AMEiS. What is it expected the dredging will cost, and what depth will be attained?
I have not an accurate estimate of the cost, but it is expected to give 22 feet depth at low tide. The dredging will be continued gradually.
It is a question whether the dredging or the pier should be the first work to accomplish. After the pier has been built, you cannot approach it on account of the lack of dredging.
The department could not do both at once.
The pier will wear out before the dredging is completed.

When the department decided to build the wharf the dredging was provided for. For the last ten years, in the maritime provinces, we have been asking for more dredges. We could not get them. Fortunately, the present Minister of Public Works has not waited to have more dredges built, and he has asked for tenders to do dredging which will improve the north shore of New Brunswick.
Mr. AMEtS. We are entitled to know about what the engineering estimate is of the cost of making the Caraquet pier approachable by vessels.

The hon. gentleman from York, says that the wharf had been used to dry one fishing net. Of course there are a great many fishing nets in Gloucester county. We just heard an hon. member from Prince Edward Island complaining that the Caraquet fleet fills up Tig-nish harbour in his province.	All these
schooners have been using the wharf. There are to-day sixteen feet at low water in that channel right along the bar. which has to be dredged before ocean steamers can come in. Meanwhile the coasting trade and the fishing fleet are benefited by the wharf. We have also other services that will be benefited. But the main object in view is to connect the wharf with the Caraquet railroad, scarcely a mile away, and the Caraquet wharf has been built with the idea of connecting it with the railway. The moment that is done, there are millions of feet of lumber waiting to use this wharf, which is the only one that they can use. I have in my pocket letters from lumber manufacturers complaining that the wharf is not yet connected with the railroad. I suppose that is the business of the railway company, but perhaps they were waiting until the dredging was done. The moment that connection is made trade will be developed. To-day the lumber interest is suffering on that account. When that connection is built Caraquet will be one of the best harbours in the maritime provinces. No doubt the movement in the maritime provinces in favour of the federal government taking over the branch lines in connection with the Intercolonial Railway, has had some influence upon the owners of the Caraquet Railway, who in that case would avoid the expenditure of this construction.

I hope the hon. member does not understand me as objecting to the construction of the wharf. I am only asking for information. I had the pleasure of visiting Caraquet wharf last year, and I I know its location, and I know the work

that is constructed there, in a place where uoubtless it will serve a large community. But the question which arose in my mind was this : Until the dredging is done the wharf can only be approached by small boats. Now, when is the dredging going to be done, and what estimate has been made of the cost of dredging so that the wharf can be approached? We know that a considerable expenditure has been made upon the wharf ; now, how much is it going to cost to make that wharf of real service to the neighbourhood? There is no use of putting the railroad down there until the dredging is done.
, Mr. TURGEON. Small vessels can come in now, but big vessels drawing 24 feet will not attempt it.
What is the depth of water over the bar?
Sixteen feet to-day, at low7 tide.

Works stated it would cost $20. In the following year the minister stated that the title to the right of way down to the wharf had been obtained at a cost of $20 Now we discover, in 1908, that the question is still open and that this unsettled claim alone amounts to $400. I would impress upon the minister the importance of having the claim of Mrs. Blackhall dealt with. If it was the agreement that the department was to pay her $400 for the title, the department should carry out that agreement and not let the interests of anv political partisan interfere.
The department will not let the interest of anv political partisan interfere.
Will the minister say that he will look into that and let us know w'hat agreement was made with Mrs. Blackhall ?
Yes.
I see that Mr. Byrne charges $173.90 for legal services.

I think vessels drawing 18 feet can come in.
. Mr. PUGSLEY. I cannot give off-hand information of the cost of the dredging. We have had a preliminary examination made, but it would be largely guess work to say the cost of the dredging. I could not come to it within $20,000 or $25,000.

Will the minister explain why it is that the department is building a wharf on the Petitcodiac river and that the department refuses to bear the whole cost of wharfs on the St. John river ?
I cannot give that to my hon. friend to-night but I will get it from the Department of Justice and give it to him before we get through with the Public Works Estimates.

When this matter was first submitted to parliament in 1902, I see by Hansard ' that when the question was asked in reference to the ownership of the land upon which the wharf was to be constructed the then Minister of Public Mr. AMES.

With regard to the St. John river, the department has been pursuing the custom which was inaugurated some fifteen years ago, in the time of the previous government, when the hon. member for North Toronto was Minister of Finance. Previous to that the Dominion government had not built wharfs on the St. John river. The hon. member for North Toronto inaugurated that policy and it has been pursued from that time down to the present.
I understand the policy has been to construct wharfs only on tidal waters.

I am telling the hon. gentleman what the policy has been with regard to the St. John river. X am not drawing any distinction between the, St. John river and tidal rivers because the tide does rise and fail in the St. John river to a limited extent up to iSpringhjll or Fredericton. All I am saying is that the policy of the Dominion government, paying half of the cost of wharfs on the St. John river, was inaugurated some 15 years ago when the hon. member for North Toronto was Minister of Finance. That policy has been pursued from that time down to the present, and in later years this government has been contributing more frequently towards wharfs on the St. John river than before, Since I have become minister I have not refused to build wharfs there. On the contrary, in addition to carrying out and continuing the policy of paying half the cost of such wharfs as the provincial government may undertake. I am prepared to ask my colleagues to allow me to go still further and to build some wharfs absolutely at the expense of the federal government so as to give reasonable accommodation to the people living alone- that very important highway.
Harbours, rivers and bridges generally-repairs and improvements, $17,000.

I would like to ask the minister what is the method when work is
done by day's labour. Who appoints the foreman ?
The foreman is appointed by the minister after inquiry as to his qualification arid reference to the resident engineer.
On whose suggestion is the foreman appointed ?

The minister appoints him. Inquiry will be made of the inember for the county supporting the government. He is usually asked to name an experienced and reliable man for the position, he makes a recommendation and then the minister causes inquiry to be made independently as to his qualifications.

I want to ask the minister whether it is customary to send a letter of this character to the resident engineer. This is a letter dated May 4, 1907 :
Sir,-I am directed by the hon. minister to authorize you to proceed by day labour with the works at the following places, for which appropriations have been granted by parliament, during the session just ended. Will you please apply to the persons mentioned for the names of competent foremen or for any other information you may require in connection with the works in their respective counties.
Then follows the county and the name of the local member.
You will please bear in mind that the above mentioned sum must, on no account, be overexpended, and I would ask you to give positive instructions to the foremen to that effect. The foremen are to be paid at the rate of $2.50 per day, unless you are otherwise instructed.
In other words, there issues, at least in the province of Quebec, a departmental letter signed by the chief engineer instructing the local resident engineer to supply the- foremen for all the works that are to be done by day's labour and instructing the local engineer to apply to the local member provided he is a good supporter of this government, for these foremen. That is the case with regard to all the day's work practically that is carried on in Quebec. I want to know if in the province of New Brunswick the same method is adopted and whether the local members who represent the counties of New Brunswick have an absolutely free hand in naming the foremen without any reference to the engineer. The local member having the naming of the foreman none but the faithful will be asked to work under him. Is it a fact that the whole pay-roll in New Brunswick is made up of the friends of the local member as is the ease in the province of Quebec ?

The same rule prevails now^as has always prevailed since confederation. Where a public work is done by the day and the amount is small the resident engineer is instructed to inquire of the local member supporting the government for the name of a competent, reliable, suitable man to act as foreman of the work. If that man is found not to be efficient and watchful the resident engineer has it impressed upon him that it is his duty to inform the department at once, and then the engineer would be authorized to make another appointment. I presume it is the same in Quebec as in New Brunswick. We do consult our friends as to the appointment and we always endeavour to get reliable men. If the work is important a recommendation is made to the minister and the minister makes inquiry as to the suitability and reliability of the appointee.

In this case it is not merely a suggestion from the local member, but the department writes to the resident engineer :
I am directed by the hon. minister to authorize you to apply to the local member for the nanje of a competent foreman.
The engineer has no discretion there ; the local member is the czar of the situation.
If the foreman is not efficient the resident engineer knows his duty.
Could you cite a case in which the foreman was ever dismissed where the local member did not consent to it?
Yes.
I would like to know it.

I wish to put myself on record as absolutely and utterly opposed to a system under which it is said to the local member :	Whenever a public work
is to be carried out in your constituency the resident engineer has to apply to you to name a political friend to put in charge of the expenditure of that money. That principle is entirely wrong. Foremen should be chosen by the department entirely because of their ability and efficiency without interference on the part of the local member.'
I don't suppose the hon. gentleman would confer with his opponents.

Under this -system nine-tenths of the money is expended for no other than political purposes and a large share of it is absolutely squandered because a foreman knows he is a political appointee and those under him know they are appointed by political favouritism. The whole system is rotten and corrupt right straight through. If we are going to construct by day's work let it be done in a businesslike way. For the department to send out a letter of that kind is carrying the patronage system to an extent which is utterly demoralizing, which gives us wretched work and which makes the Department of Public Works a political machine and nothing else.

The very system which the hon. member (Mr. Arnes) has denounced so vehemently was rampant under the Conservative administration. I know a case in which the representative of the county was in opposition to the Dominion government, the local member happened to be a friend of the party in power and all these works had to be carried out under the dictation as well as the direction of the local member and that was done under the Conservative regime.
We are' supposed to be advancing in civilization.
If you get good honest work there can be no objection.
But you don't.

We do get honest and faithful service.
Lower Newcastle-wharf on Miramichi river, $2,000.
What will be the cost?

The probable cost $2,300 to be done by days work.
Madawaska river-extension of dyke on east side of river at Edmundston southward, $10,000.

Contract let May 20 last, to be completed May 20, 1909, contract price, $10,440.
How is it you make an expenditure on a tributary of the St. John and you will not make an expenditure on the St. John river itself?

We do make expenditures on the St. John river.
Moncton wharf-enlargement of, $16,000.
When was the contract let?
Two or three months ago. Four tenders received; lowest $14,925 and highest $19,765.
How does the department come to build this wharf at Moncton?
For the public convenience.

There is more traffic and more navigation at Fredericton than at Moncton, and I do not think the city of Fredericton ever had the advantage of a wharf being built by the government. In these estimates three wharfs are provided on the Petitcodiac, and yet the minister justifies the government in refusing to pay the cost of these wharfs on the St. John river.
What is the use of saying that? The government is paying for the wharfs on the St. John river, and proposes to do it more than ever.

The government is not doing it. We have this year in the estimates for the St. John river the statement: * Contributions to local government not to exceed one-half the first cost of local wharfs.' Why is there a discrimination made against the St. John river and in favour of the Petitcodiac ?
Do you oppose this item?

I am not opposing the item, but I want a square deal for the St. John river. I find appropriation after appropriation going through for wharfs in every other river, but when it comes to the St. John river, which is so important from the standpoint of the business interests of New Brunswick, this government takes the position that the local administration should

build the wharfs. The minister may say what he likes about his willingness and his policy in that regard, but he did take the position the other day that it was still uij to the government of New Brunswick to go on building wharfs on the St. John, and the most he was prepared to do-to use his own sweet words-was ' perhaps increase to a reasonable extent the grants that had been made.'
You would not expect me to Increase them to an unreasonable extent?

I would expect you to do what you promised the people in the last election campaign. There the hon. minister made several speeches and many promises. He said it was unjust to the province that it should have to build its own wharfs when the other provinces were having them built out of the federal treasury. That is the injustice we complain of. We complain that we are not in the same position as the other provinces, and until the Minister of Public Works provides for the building of all the wharfs required on the St. John river out of the federal treasury, that Injustice will stand.
When did it first dawn on you that there was an injustice in this particular?

Ever since I have been in this parliament I have protested against it. I have drawn it to the attention of the Minister of Public Works every session. I have here a declaration made by the minister at Chatham in the last election when addressing a public meeting. He said :
Another advantage to be accrued from the two governments working in harmony would be the relieving of the province from maintaining the wharfs in these waters. Thus more money would be released for roads and bridges.
The minister pointed out that it was plainly conditioned on the people condoning his manifold offences in administering their local affairs and continuing in office a government with which he could work in harmony, that he would build their wharfs. But I venture to say he will not take that position in this House. He promised the people of New Brunswick that they would be relieved of the expense of building and maintaining their wharfs and be put in that respect in the same position as the other provinces, and until he does that he cannot make much claim on their consideration. It should not make any difference whether the people of New Brunswick have refused to continue in office a government with which he himself could have worked very harmoniously. It has, however, been discovered since, on examining the public accounts of that province, that the harmony was more profitable to the minister than the people.
Richibucto-extension of piers, &c., $3,300.
Is that under contract ?

Mr. John Jardine had the contract for the main work which has been completed. The contract was for $17,000. This is for a small extension.
River St. John, including tributaries, $2,000.
River St. John, wharfs and tide water-contribution to local government, not to exceed one-half of cost of wharfs built by it, $5,000.

I wish to point out, as I did last session, the condition of St. John I'iver channel between Fredericton and Woodstock. A year ago I called attention to the need of deepening this channel and my hon. friend from Carleton supported my demand. The then acting Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fisher) promised to take the matter up, and I believe did so. I furnished him with a memo, of the several points along the river where dredging was required. The matter was referred to the resident engineer, but since the present minister has taken office nothing has been done. I have been in correspondence with him and was very much surprised to receive a letter from him in April last saying he was not convinced that any improvement could be made without the expenditure of a very large sum. In 1902 a dredge was built to be used exclusively for low water work in the St. John river. That was in the late Mr. Tarte's time. It was put at work on Springhill but was shortly moved down the river and nothing has been done, since. There are many places in the channel between Fredericton and Woodstock which require clearing and deepening. As a result of the neglect of the government in this matter the people living along the valley of that river have been deprived of their only means of communication between Woodstock and Fredericton, as the boat had to be withdrawn because of the condition of the channel and the impossibility of making more than 15 or 20 trips in a season. The minister, when attorney general of New Brunswick, and in the campaign to which I have referred, said that the interests of the people in that section were very dear to his heart. These people expected to have the advantage of being on the line of the Transcontinental Railway. This they feel they were unjustly deprived of by this government, and now, in consequence of the neglect of the river channel by the government, they have lost their only means of communication between Fredericton and Woodstock.
'Mr. PUGSLEY. My hon. friend will be pleased to know that some time ago I received a memorial from the town of Woodstock which was presented by the member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) who urged upon me the necessity of making these improvements. Recently I was waited on

again by that gentleman and by an influential gentleman from Fredericton who again pressed the matter and convinced me of the desirability of taking early steps for the purpose of determining whether or not it is possible by the expenditure of a reasonable amount to improve the navigation of the river. I have much pleasure in saying that during the present year I intend to put an engineering staff at work there to ascertain if it is possible to improve the navigation at a reasonable cost.
